title: US States Move to Strip Data Center Tax Breaks as $64 Billion in Projects Stall
excerpt: At least nine states are considering full repeal of sales tax exemptions for data centers, with Virginia alone forgoing $1.6 billion in revenue annually as communities revolt over electricity costs and water use.
body:
• More than 300 U.S. local and state governments have enacted bans, moratoriums, or restrictions on new data center development since 2023, blocking or delaying roughly $64 billion in projects.
  • At least nine states — including Georgia, Michigan, and Pennsylvania — have considered bills to fully repeal data center sales tax exemptions, according to a National Conference of State Legislatures report.
  • New York became the first state to halt construction outright in July 2026, with Governor Kathy Hochul signing an executive order barring new permits for facilities of 50 megawatts or larger.
  • The cost of tax exemptions has ballooned: Virginia lost $1.6 billion in sales tax revenue in fiscal year 2025 — 16 times initial projections — while Texas surpassed $1 billion and Georgia's exemptions jumped from $10 million in 2020 to $625 million this year.

The rapid expansion of data centers across the United States is running headlong into a wall of state and local resistance, with lawmakers from both parties moving to repeal billions of dollars in tax incentives that once lured the AI-powered facilities to their jurisdictions.

Of the 38 states that currently offer data center tax incentives, lawmakers in two dozen have introduced proposals to repeal or substantially curtail them, according to a report by the National Conference of State Legislatures. The shift marks a dramatic reversal for an industry that has enjoyed generous subsidies for more than a decade.

The Price Tag Comes Into Focus

The numbers driving the backlash are staggering. Virginia, the world's largest data center market, lost $1.6 billion in sales tax revenue in fiscal year 2025 from data center exemptions — roughly 16 times what the state originally projected when the program launched, according to Bloomberg Tax. Texas surpassed $1 billion in foregone revenue the same year, against an initial estimate of $130 million. Georgia's exemption costs exploded from $10 million in 2020 to $625 million this year, while Illinois saw its foregone revenue soar to $370 million from $10 million over just four years.

"It's a very different beast than anything else we've seen before."

— Kasia Tarczynska, Senior Research Analyst, Good Jobs First

Tarczynska's organization, an advocacy group that tracks state and local subsidies, has called for ending data center tax breaks, arguing that unlike traditional manufacturing plants with hundreds of on-site jobs, data centers create "very few jobs and very little economic development."

States Draw New Battle Lines

The most dramatic action came from New York, where Governor Kathy Hochul in July 2026 signed an executive order temporarily barring the state from approving new permits for data center facilities of 50 megawatts or larger. "Progress shouldn't arrive with a higher utility bill, deleted water supply, or noise pollution," Hochul said at a press conference in Brooklyn. Her office is also considering requiring data centers to pay into a fund supporting the state's electrical grid.

As many as 15 states are considering moratoriums similar to New York's, according to the NCSL. Ohio Governor Mike DeWine announced a pause on hearing new requests for data center tax breaks while a state commission studies the issue. Illinois Governor JB Pritzker suspended new exemption agreements after lawmakers failed to repeal the state's program. Washington eliminated its sales tax break on equipment used to refurbish existing data centers, a move the state estimates will generate $143.9 million in the 2027-29 biennium.

Michigan created its data center tax exemption only in 2024, yet a bipartisan group of lawmakers is already seeking to scrap it entirely. In Georgia, Republican state Senator Greg Brass led an effort to end the state's exemption for future projects after living near a data center that drew mixed community support.

"You're still more than welcome to come here. You're just gonna pay, just like everyone else."

— Sen. Greg Brass, Georgia State Senate

Local Resistance Goes Nationwide

The pushback extends far beyond state capitols. More than 300 local and state governments have enacted bans, moratoriums, or restrictions on new data center development since 2023, according to a report from The Information. Roughly $64 billion in U.S. data center projects have been either blocked or delayed, with $18 billion blocked outright and another $46 billion delayed. As of mid-June 2026, 97 moratoriums remained actively in effect across the country.

A Gallup poll released in May found that seven in 10 Americans do not want data centers built near them, with respondents citing concerns about secrecy, land use, and excessive consumption of water and electricity. The Department of Energy's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates that by 2030, data centers could consume between 9.5 and 15.3 percent of all U.S. electricity, up from about 4.4 percent today.

The industry is fighting back. The Data Center Coalition nearly tripled its lobbying spend in the third quarter of 2025, according to federal lobbying disclosures. A new AI trade group has been distributing talking points to members of Congress and organizing local data center field trips, according to Politico.

What It Means for Tech and Indian IT

Rising data center costs could ripple through the cloud computing ecosystem. Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud — the three hyperscalers that dominate the market — are among the largest beneficiaries of state tax incentives. Higher costs could eventually translate into increased cloud service pricing, which would directly affect the operations of Indian IT services giants like TCS, Infosys, and Wipro, all of which rely heavily on U.S. cloud infrastructure for client delivery.

Looking Ahead

Congressional action may be on the horizon. At a recent House hearing, Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie said he was committed to finding "common ground" on data center energy costs. "We all want to make sure that locals don't bear the burden of the energy needs of data centers," he said. An Ohio ballot initiative to ban new data centers altogether — a sign of escalating public discontent — is currently circulating for signatures.

The outcome of these battles will shape where and how quickly the United States builds the infrastructure underpinning its AI ambitions, with the 2026 midterm elections adding political urgency to a debate that shows no sign of cooling.
